---
title: "Metric Tree"
description: "How measures compose, decomposing a top-line metric into the drivers that explain it"
---

While a single measure is only a fact, the **Metric Tree** captures how
measures *relate* to one another, so that a top-line metric such as ARR,
labor cost %, or contribution margin decomposes into the driver metrics that
explain it. It is the part of the [World Model](/guide/build/world-model)
that turns "what happened" into "why," and because it is built entirely from
your [semantic model](/guide/build/semantic-model/simple-model) definitions,
there is no separate file to maintain.

## How measures compose

Measures connect through two kinds of edges, which differ in what they claim.

### Component edges

When one measure's expression references another with `{{view.measure}}`,
that reference *is* an edge: `arr` depends on `net_mrr`, which in turn depends
on `total_mrr` and `churned_mrr`, forming a tree the engine reads straight from
the formulas. The operator in front of each reference (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`)
tells it whether the relationship is additive or multiplicative.

```yaml
measures:
  - name: net_mrr
    type: number
    expr: "{{revenue.total_mrr}} - {{revenue.churned_mrr}}"
  - name: arr
    type: number
    expr: "{{revenue.net_mrr}} * 12"
```

### Driver edges

Where component edges are arithmetic, **driver edges** (declared with
`drivers:`) encode the causal map, stating which metrics push a target up or
down, in which direction, and how confident you are that the relationship is
real.

```yaml
measures:
  - name: arr
    type: number
    expr: "{{revenue.net_mrr}} * 12"
    drivers:
      - measure: revenue.churn_rate
        direction: negative
        confidence: high
        description: "Higher churn directly reduces ARR"
      - measure: revenue.arpu
        direction: positive
        description: "ARPU expansion drives ARR growth"
```

Driver edges are deliberately **qualitative**, stating what drives what
without claiming how much. A magnitude is a causal claim, and observational
data cannot reliably support one, because a coefficient fitted from history
absorbs everything that happened to move alongside it. Magnitudes come from
the control layer instead: when a [control](/guide/build/world-model/controls)
acts on a driver, [evaluation](/guide/build/world-model/evaluation) estimates
the driver's effect from the interventions themselves, and that estimate
becomes the authoritative one. An edge that no control acts on either stays
qualitative or carries an observational estimate that is labeled as weak.

## Promotion up the hierarchy

Because the [entity graph](/guide/build/semantic-model/entities) defines a
`parent:` hierarchy (sale → store → company → market), a measure defined once
at the sale grain automatically **promotes** upward, so `markets.net_sales` is
derived by rolling up `sales.net_sales` rather than being redefined. The tree
therefore captures not only *how* metrics compose but also *every level of the
business* at which they apply.

## Explore it in the IDE

The Metric Tree is a tab in the Semantic Model IDE, where it renders your
measures as an interactive graph laid out from the top down:

- **Composite** nodes (the metrics built from others) are highlighted,
  **driver** nodes are tinted amber, and leaf inputs are muted.
- **Component edges** are drawn solid, while **driver edges** are dashed and
  animated, and appear fainter when confidence is low.
- Clicking a measure selects it, dimming unrelated edges and opening a side
  panel with the measure's definition and its **ranked drivers**, sorted by
  influence.

## What you can do with it

Because the tree knows how every metric is built, it powers four operations
over your metrics:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Sensitivity" icon="ranking-star">
    Rank the drivers of any measure by how much they move it, using the best
    available magnitude on each edge: control-learned where a control acts,
    labeled observational estimates elsewhere.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Predict" icon="wand-magic-sparkles">
    What-if propagation: change a driver by some delta and see the estimated
    impact ripple up to the top-line metric, carrying each edge's confidence.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Explain (RCA)" icon="magnifying-glass">
    Decompose a metric's period-over-period change across its drivers and the
    segments that concentrate it, with warnings for Simpson's paradox and
    offsetting effects. Anomalies surface in the Insights Inbox with an
    AI-authored root cause. **Available today.**
  </Card>
  <Card title="Opportunity" icon="arrow-trend-up">
    Size the gap between each segment and its benchmark, and propagate the top
    opportunity through the tree. **Available today.** See
    [Opportunity sizing](/guide/build/world-model/opportunity-sizing).
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

For example, an `explain` on `labor_cost_pct` for a location might read:

```text
Labor cost: 37.5%  (13% lower than average)

Root cause
  revenue          +25% vs average
  labor            +50% vs average
  employees        ~ average
  overtime hours   +100% vs average

Recommendation:  investigate overtime cost at the San Mateo location
```
